highlights:
The eight things production serverless GPU inference needs, from a warm floor and a spend ceiling to retries, private auth and metrics, and how to set each on fal Serverless.

Jim Cai· Published Nov 3, 2026· 7 min read

A serverless GPU provider is ready for production when you can control eight things: the warm floor and the ceiling, cold starts, multi-GPU runners, logs and exportable metrics, what happens when a request fails, where it runs and what capacity backs it, who can call it, and the most it can cost per hour. On fal Serverless each one is a setting on your app class, and this page shows which.

...

Keep staging apart from production with environments: `fal deploy --env staging` deploys a separate app with its own secrets. 16 Deploys are rolling by default. fal starts a runner on the new revision and switches traffic only when it is healthy. Every deploy is a revision, and you can roll back to any earlier one. 17 

## Pricing you can predict

fal Serverless bills per second while a runner is alive. Setup, idle, running, draining and teardown are billed. Waiting for hardware and pulling the image are not. Prices on fal.ai/pricing, per GPU-hour:

| GPU | VRAM | List price | As low as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B300 | 288 GB | $12.99/h | $5.99/h |
| B200 | 192 GB | $7.99/h | $5.49/h |
| H200 | 141 GB | $6.00/h | $2.99/h |
| H100 | 80 GB | $4.50/h | $2.49/h |
| RTX PRO 6000 | 96 GB | $4.00/h | $1.99/h |

"As low as" rates are quoted through fal's sales team. Two numbers make a budget predictable:

- The most you can spend per hour is `max_concurrency` × `num_gpus` × the hourly rate. An app capped at 10 single-H100 runners cannot cost more than $45 an hour at list price. A rollout can briefly start replacement runners above the cap.
- The cost of a warm floor is `min_concurrency` × the hourly rate × 24 hours. One H100 held warm costs $108 a day at list price.

If your GPUs are busy most of the day, part of the traffic may be cheaper on reserved capacity. This break-even guide works it out.

results.title: NVIDIA B200 Price in 2026: Specs and GPU Pricing | fal
results.author: Jim Cai
highlights:
# NVIDIA B200 Price in 2026: Specs, Hourly Rates and Reserved Capacity

The NVIDIA B200 pairs 192 GB of HBM3e with 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth and native FP4. This guide covers its specs, the three ways B200 time is priced (hourly, per second, reserved), and fal's published B200 rate with worked cost examples.

Jim Cai· Updated Oct 19, 2026· 9 min read

The NVIDIA B200 is the first-generation Blackwell data-center GPU: 192 GB HBM3e, 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth, NVLink 5 and native FP4. Few teams buy one outright, so the price that matters is the rental rate. B200 time is sold three ways: an hourly list rate, per-second billing on serverless platforms, and lower reserved or committed rates. On fal Serverless a B200 costs $7.99 per GPU-hour at list price, billed per second only while a runner is alive, and as low as $5.49 per GPU-hour with committed capacity.

...

### Hourly (on-demand) rates

The headline number is an hourly price per GPU. Two questions decide what you actually pay at that rate:

- What is the smallest unit you can rent? Some offers only rent whole 8-GPU servers, so the real hourly price is eight times the per-GPU rate.
- What is the billing granularity? Hourly billing rounds up. A 10-minute test on an hourly plan costs a full hour.

### Per-second (serverless) billing

Serverless platforms bill per second for the time your workload holds a GPU. Per-second billing makes the hourly rate a ceiling rather than a floor. If traffic is bursty and runners scale down between bursts, you pay only for the seconds a runner is alive.

On fal Serverless, a runner is billed while it is in the SETUP, IDLE, RUNNING, DRAINING and TERMINATING states. Time spent waiting for hardware (PENDING) and pulling your container image (DOCKER_PULL) is not billed, and requests that fail with a 5xx error are not charged. 6 A deployment that scales to zero runners has no compute charge. Multi-GPU runners are billed as GPU count multiplied by duration. 6 

### Reserved and committed capacity

The lowest B200 rates come from a commitment: reserved runners, a spend commitment or a longer contract. You trade flexibility for a lower per-hour price and guaranteed capacity. Reserved pricing makes the most sense when your baseline traffic keeps GPUs busy around the clock. Many teams combine a reserved baseline with per-second capacity on top for peaks.

## fal's B200 price

Prices as of October 19, 2026, taken from fal.ai/pricing. 7 Check that page for the current rate before you plan a budget.

| GPU | VRAM | List price | As low as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | 192 GB | $7.99/h | $5.49/h |

The list price is the per-GPU hourly rate, billed per second while a runner is alive. The "as low as" rate depends on your capacity arrangement, such as reserved runners or a usage commitment. Contact sales for those terms.

At the list price, one B200 second costs about $0.00222. Some worked examples:

| Workload | Billed GPU time | Cost at list price | Cost at "as low as" |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10-minute test run on 1 GPU | 600 GPU-seconds | $1.33 | $0.92 |
| 1 hour on an 8-GPU runner | 8 GPU-hours | $63.92 | $43.92 |
| 1 GPU kept warm for a 30-day month | 720 GPU-hours | $5,752.80 | $3,952.80 |
| Bursty traffic: 3 runner-hours a day, 30 days | 90 GPU-hours | $719.10 | $494.10 |

The last two rows show why scaling to zero matters as much as the hourly rate. The same B200 costs one-eighth as much per month when it runs only while traffic needs it.

### B200 or H200 on price

Most inference is limited by memory bandwidth, so the hourly price per TB/s of bandwidth is a rough guide to cost per output. Using fal's published rates: 5 7 

| GPU | Memory bandwidth | List price | List price per TB/s | As low as | As low as per TB/s |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | 8 TB/s | $7.99/h | $1.00 | $5.49/h | $0.69 |
| H200 | 4.8 TB/s | $6.00/h | $1.25 | $2.99/h | $0.62 |
| H100 | 3.35 TB/s | $4.50/h | $1.34 | $2.49/h | $0.74 |

At list prices the B200 is the cheapest of the three per unit of bandwidth. At the lowest committed rates the H200 is slightly cheaper, so if you are committing to capacity for a model that fits in 141 GB, benchmark both before you choose.

...

### How much does an NVIDIA B200 cost?

NVIDIA does not publish a list price for the B200, and it is mostly sold inside 8-GPU servers, so for most teams the useful number is the rental rate. On fal Serverless a B200 costs $7.99 per GPU-hour at list price, billed per second, and as low as $5.49 per GPU-hour with reserved capacity or a usage commitment. These rates are as of October 19, 2026; current rates are on fal.ai/pricing.

Yes. Reserved runners and usage commitments lower the effective rate from the $7.99/h list price toward the "as low as" rate of $5.49/h (as of October 19, 2026). Contact the fal sales team for terms.

## Pick a GPU in one line

Pick the smallest GPU your model fits on. fal's published rates, billed per second: 11 

| GPU | `machine_type` | VRAM | List price | As low as |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RTX PRO 6000 | `GPU-RTXPRO6000` | 96 GB | $4.00/h | $1.99/h |
| H100 | `GPU-H100` | 80 GB | $4.50/h | $2.49/h |
| H200 | `GPU-H200` | 141 GB | $6.00/h | $2.99/h |
| B200 | `GPU-B200` | 192 GB | $7.99/h | $5.49/h |

"As low as" rates are quoted through fal's sales team. To fall back when a type is busy, give a list: `machine_type = ["GPU-H100", "GPU-H200"]`. fal tries them in order.

## Scale to zero, and when not to

A new app scales to zero by default: `min_concurrency` is 0. 12 After a request, an idle runner stays up for `keep_alive` seconds (60 by default), then shuts down. With no runners alive, nothing is billed. 13 

Billing covers the time a runner is alive: setup, idle, running, draining and teardown. Waiting for a GPU and pulling the image are not billed. Requests that fail with an HTTP 5xx status are not charged.

The cost of scale to zero is a cold start on the next request. If users cannot wait, keep one runner warm with `min_concurrency = 1`. On an H100 at list price that is $4.50 an hour, all day. Raise `max_concurrency` (2 by default) before real traffic arrives. For the trade-offs, see What Is a Serverless GPU Cold Start?.

### GPU types and price

Match memory to your model first, then match speed to your latency target. A model that does not fit in one GPU's memory needs a multi-GPU runner, and every GPU in it is billed for the whole time the runner is alive:

Runner cost per hour = number of GPUs × per-GPU hourly rate

For example, a model that needs 120 GB of GPU memory does not fit on one H100 (80 GB). On two H100s it costs 2 × $4.50 = $9.00 per hour. On one H200 (141 GB) it costs $6.00 per hour, a third less, even though the H200 has the higher hourly rate. So price the smallest set of GPUs your model fits on, not the cheapest GPU.

Cost per request = hourly rate ÷ 3,600 × billed seconds per request ÷ requests served at once per runner.
